narrative:
Full passive sweep against inDrive (HackerOne bug_bounty, $50–$15k, 113 in-scope assets, Core/Non-core split). Bucket-hunter tested 75 candidates; 3 exist (`indrive` us-east-1, `indrive-files` us-west-2, `indrive-test` ap-southeast-1). All three are private (list 403). Secret-hunter ran trufflehog Passes A+B+C against 2 inDriver org repos (handbook, UDF) plus 1 fan mirror; noseyparker scanned the same 3 repos for historical pattern matches. Result: 0 verified secrets, 0 noseyparker matches, 0 candidates of any kind. Ownership-verifier ran on all 3 existing buckets: `indrive-files` → unowned (clean A=neg + B=neg + C=inc, aggregation-override rule fired correctly); `indrive` → unknown; `indrive-test` → unknown. Net reportable findings: 0.

The `indrive-files` unowned verdict was a clean win for the aggregation-override rule (rule-ownership_verifier-bucket_aggregation_override-1c25c from the 8x8 engagement). GH returned 0 results for `indrive-files`, wayback word-boundary returned 0 hits across 15,426 archived URLs, and DNS was a generic AWS CNAME — the rule correctly promoted the verdict from unknown to unowned, saving a manual triage decision.

The `indrive` bucket exposed a residual gap in the word_boundary wayback rule. The rule (from mercadolibre) was already live and was applied correctly: word_boundary mode grepped for `\bindrive\b` across 15,426 archived URLs. It still returned 10,627 hits — not because word_boundary failed, but because the brand stem 'indrive' appears verbatim in the program's own URL paths (e.g., paths under `indrive.com` that contain the word 'indrive' as a path segment or query token). Word_boundary cannot disambiguate self-reference when the asset name equals the root brand token that the company uses everywhere in its own URLs. The `indrive` bucket is therefore structurally unresolvable via Wayback for the same reason that 'mercadolibre' was — but unlike that engagement where word_boundary recovered a useful 0-hit result, here even word_boundary saturates. This is a second data point that bare-brand-name buckets should be skipped in bucket-hunter rather than handed to ownership-verifier.

The `indrive-test` bucket produced 3 GitHub hits, none inside the inDriver org namespace: a QEMU startup script (mezmer42/bootkit), a bucket-enumeration dump by a bounty aggregator (rix4uni/BugBountyData), and a Cognito sample-data file (artista7/cognito-backend). The BugBountyData hit is the canonical signature of an external scanner picking up the name independently — it tells us nothing about who owns the bucket. Because A=ambiguous (not negative), the aggregation-override rule correctly did not fire and verdict remained unknown.

The inDriver GH org is structurally thin: 2 public repos (handbook and UDF), neither containing application source code. Pass A trufflehog scanned 2,810 chunks / 12 MB across both and returned 0 verified hits. This is not the same as the mature-org H3 signal seen on MercadoLibre (101 repos, 2.7 GB, long history) — inDriver publishes almost nothing publicly on GitHub, so the 0-verified result reflects an extremely small attack surface, not organizational hygiene over a large codebase. The 81 repos surfaced by GH code search were almost entirely brand-name noise (bug-bounty aggregators, unrelated projects). If revisiting inDrive for secrets, the meaningful sources are not on GitHub at all; consider mobile APK static analysis or traffic interception paths instead. Pass A+B+C against the org is not worth repeating.
